questions.stem: A hospital promotes annual influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel. What is the primary patient-safety rationale?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Vaccination replaces standard precautions and other respiratory infection-control measures during influenza season.","B":"Vaccination eliminates all influenza infections among healthcare personnel and patients during the season.","C":"Vaccination is used mainly to satisfy an administrative requirement unrelated to transmission prevention.","D":"Vaccination reduces influenza illness and the risk that infected healthcare personnel transmit influenza to vulnerable patients."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel as an important infection-prevention measure. Vaccination reduces influenza illness among personnel and helps reduce transmission risk to patients; it complements rather than replaces other infection-control practices.
questions.source_name: CDC — Influenza Vaccination Information for Health Care Workers
questions.source_detail: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for healthcare personnel to protect personnel and patients and reduce healthcare-associated transmission risk.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous exposure to blood from a patient with known hepatitis C virus infection. Which follow-up is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obtain recommended baseline and follow-up HCV testing because no vaccine or recommended HCV postexposure prophylaxis is available.","B":"Give hepatitis C immune globulin immediately and omit follow-up testing if the exposure site was washed promptly.","C":"Administer a hepatitis C vaccine immediately and repeat the vaccine after the occupational-health evaluation is complete.","D":"Start direct-acting antiviral treatment immediately after every exposure without first performing baseline or follow-up testing."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends baseline testing and indicated follow-up testing after occupational HCV exposure. HCV postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended, and there is no HCV vaccine. Detecting acute infection permits referral for treatment.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guidelines for Health Care Personnel Exposed to Hepatitis C Virus
questions.source_detail: Occupational HCV exposure requires baseline/follow-up testing; postexposure prophylaxis is not recommended.

questions.stem: A nurse is responsible for controlled substances on a hospital unit. Which storage practice best supports diversion prevention and accountability?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep controlled substances in an unlocked medication cart when authorized staff remain somewhere on the unit.","B":"Store controlled substances securely with access limited to authorized personnel and maintain required accountability records.","C":"Share medication-storage access credentials among staff so urgent doses can be obtained without individual authentication.","D":"Move controlled substances to an open medication shelf during busy periods and reconcile the inventory at the end of the shift."}}
questions.rationale: Controlled substances require secure storage and access controls appropriate to the setting, together with required records and accountability processes. Leaving them unsecured or sharing access credentials undermines diversion prevention.
questions.source_name: U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration — Controlled Substance Security Requirements
questions.source_detail: Controlled substances must be stored and handled under security controls that guard against theft and diversion, with access limited appropriately.

questions.stem: A client uses supplemental oxygen at home. Which instruction is most important for reducing fire risk?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keep oxygen equipment away from smoking, open flames, sparks, and other ignition sources because oxygen accelerates combustion.","B":"Smoking is acceptable if the nasal cannula is removed briefly because oxygen remaining in clothing and the environment poses no risk.","C":"Place the oxygen concentrator next to a gas stove so the client can observe the equipment while preparing meals.","D":"Use petroleum-based products around oxygen equipment because they reduce static electricity and therefore lower ignition risk."}}
questions.rationale: Oxygen itself is not flammable, but an oxygen-enriched environment allows materials to ignite more readily and burn more intensely. Home oxygen must be kept away from smoking and other ignition sources.
questions.source_name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration — Safe Use of Oxygen Equipment
questions.source_detail: Home oxygen users should avoid smoking, flames, sparks, and other ignition sources around oxygen equipment.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that an electrical medical device has a frayed power cord. What is the appropriate action?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue using the device until the current patient treatment is finished, then report the damaged cord.","B":"Remove the device from service and follow facility procedures for evaluation, repair, or replacement by qualified personnel.","C":"Wrap the damaged section with adhesive tape and return the device to routine patient-care use immediately.","D":"Repair the electrical cord personally if the device still powers on and no exposed conductor is readily visible."}}
questions.rationale: Damaged electrical cords can create shock, fire, and equipment-failure hazards. Unsafe equipment should be removed from service and managed through the organization's maintenance/equipment-safety process rather than improvised at the bedside.
questions.source_detail: Damaged electrical equipment and flexible cords must not remain in service when defects could expose users to electrical hazards.

questions.stem: A maternity unit uses matching parent-infant identification bands and additional security controls for newborns. What is the best interpretation of this practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These measures are appropriate only in hospitals located in areas with a documented high rate of violent crime.","B":"These measures are unnecessary because newborn abduction is too rare to warrant prevention procedures in hospitals.","C":"These measures provide layered safeguards against infant misidentification or abduction and supplement routine identification procedures.","D":"Electronic security controls eliminate the need for staff to verify parent-infant identification before releasing a newborn."}}
questions.rationale: Newborn security uses layered safeguards rather than a single control. Matching identification and facility security procedures reduce the risk of wrong-family release and infant abduction; technology does not replace staff verification.
questions.source_name: National Center for Missing & Exploited Children — For Healthcare Professionals
questions.source_detail: Healthcare facilities use prevention and response safeguards to reduce infant-abduction risk.

questions.stem: A client self-administers insulin at home. Which instruction about used needles is appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place used needles loose in household trash so sanitation workers can identify them during collection.","B":"Flush used needles down the toilet after each injection to prevent accidental contact by household members.","C":"Place used needles promptly in an FDA-cleared sharps container and follow community disposal requirements when the container is ready for disposal.","D":"Store used needles uncovered on a rigid tray until several have accumulated, then transfer them together to the household trash."}}
questions.rationale: FDA recommends placing used sharps immediately into an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container and following local disposal rules. Loose disposal, flushing, or leaving exposed sharps creates preventable needlestick risk.
questions.source_name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration — Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps
questions.source_detail: Used sharps should be placed immediately in FDA-cleared sharps containers and disposed of according to community guidance.

questions.stem: A nurse educator discusses the historical development of universal precautions. Which statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"CDC developed universal precautions during the HIV/AIDS era to treat blood and specified body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of known infection status.","B":"Universal precautions originated as a food-safety program and were later adapted to prevent occupational blood exposure in hospitals.","C":"Universal precautions required isolation of every hospitalized patient regardless of diagnosis, symptoms, or anticipated exposure to body fluids.","D":"Universal precautions were designed to replace hand hygiene and personal protective equipment with routine environmental disinfection alone."}}
questions.rationale: CDC's universal precautions approach emerged in the 1980s amid concern about occupational transmission of bloodborne pathogens, particularly HIV and HBV. It treated blood and certain body fluids as potentially infectious regardless of known status and later contributed to Standard Precautions.
questions.source_detail: Historical background describes Universal Precautions as an approach developed for prevention of occupational bloodborne infection and later incorporated into Standard Precautions.

questions.stem: A nurse manager evaluates whether reducing registered-nurse staffing could affect patient safety. Which finding is most consistent with the evidence base?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Lower nurse staffing has been associated with worse patient outcomes, including increased adverse events and mortality in multiple observational studies.","B":"Lower nurse staffing consistently improves patient outcomes because fewer handoffs occur between registered nurses during hospitalization.","C":"Nurse staffing affects hospital finances but has not been associated with measurable differences in patient safety or clinical outcomes.","D":"Patient outcomes are independent of nurse staffing as long as the unit maintains the same number of occupied inpatient beds."}}
questions.rationale: A substantial observational evidence base links lower registered-nurse staffing with worse outcomes, including adverse events and mortality. The evidence supports staffing as a patient-safety factor, although individual studies do not establish that staffing is the sole cause of every outcome.
questions.source_name: AHRQ Patient Safety Network — Nursing and Patient Safety
questions.source_detail: Evidence reviews associate nurse staffing and workload with patient safety outcomes, including mortality and adverse events.

questions.stem: A nurse applies transcultural nursing principles when planning care for a client whose cultural background differs from the nurse's. Which action best reflects this approach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the same care plan for every client because modifying care for cultural preferences creates inconsistent nursing standards.","B":"Base the plan on assumptions about the client's cultural group without asking the individual client about preferences or practices.","C":"Exclude cultural practices from the plan whenever biomedical treatment is available, even when the practices do not conflict with safety.","D":"Assess the client's individual cultural values and practices and incorporate relevant preferences into safe, clinically appropriate care."}}
questions.rationale: Culturally congruent nursing care requires individualized assessment rather than stereotyping. Relevant cultural values, beliefs, and practices can be incorporated into care when compatible with patient safety and clinical needs.
questions.source_name: HHS Office of Minority Health — National CLAS Standards
questions.source_detail: Culturally and linguistically appropriate services call for respectful, responsive care that addresses individual cultural health beliefs and practices.
